Orbits and fields of definition for graded Keller maps

K. Kistner Email address: kyle@ulam.capital and T. Shaska Email address: shaska@oakland.edu
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

In [21] were proposed classifying equivariant polynomial maps by the signature of the weight vector, and asked which hyperbolic weights carry graded Keller counterexamples and how the nonempty ones are stratified. We construct two families. Cyclic cones populate (1,−1,−1)(1,-1,-1) at every composite generic fibre degree N≥6N\geq 6, with a six-sheeted member over ℚ⁡(−15)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-15}) and a 3333-sheeted member over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. A diagonal family gives 𝒦⁡(3,(1,−p,−p))≠∅\mathcal{K}(3,(1,-p,-p))\neq\emptyset for every p≥2p\geq 2, with detJ​Fp=−p\det JF_{p}=-p and odd generic fibre degree 2​p−12p-1. The geometric monodromy of every member of both families is alternating or symmetric of full degree, so the solvable case of [21] occurs only at generic degree three.

At generic degree twelve the normalized quartic cyclic seeds are cut out by a smooth plane cubic EE over ℚ\mathbb{Q} whose points give pairwise distinct 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp}-orbits. Two of the associated quotient covers are left-right equivalent exactly when J=9​b2/(8​a​c)J=9b^{2}/(8ac) agrees, and J:E→ℙ1J\colon E\to\mathbb{P}^{1} has degree six: it forgets the lift-point marking. Hence a generic quotient class has six graded lifts, 𝒦⁡(3,(1,−1,−1))\mathcal{K}(3,(1,-1,-1)) carries infinitely many orbits, and quotient invariants are not complete for graded classification. An alternating-shear member lies in a separate stratum, with monodromy A12A_{12} and branch semigroup ⟨6,26,27⟩\langle 6,26,27\rangle against ⟨4,11⟩\langle 4,11\rangle; its braid orbit is unique, of size 7654576545, and its arithmetic monodromy over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is S12S_{12} with constants extension ℚ⁡(−3)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3}).

We resolve the flagship bounded scheme of the original counterexample scheme-theoretically: 𝒴1,2,(4,3,1),K∘≅𝒢K×Spec⁡K⁡[η]/(η2)\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{1,2,(4,3,1),K}\cong\mathcal{G}_{K}\times\Spec K[\eta]/(\eta^{2}) equivariantly for the degree-bound-preserving gauge group 𝒢=Blin×(𝔾m)3\mathcal{G}=B_{\mathrm{lin}}\times(\mathbb{G}_{m})^{3}, so its reduction is a single orbit and its orbit quotient is the dual point. Finally, the second lift condition is the vanishing of ∫0ϵφ​(W)k​W−2​𝑑W\int_{0}^{\epsilon}\varphi(W)^{k}W^{-2}\,dW with ϵ=(−1)k\epsilon=(-1)^{k}. It has no solution over a field with a real embedding when kk is even, and at k=2k=2 it diagonalizes over ℚ\mathbb{Q} as ⟨3,5,…,2​n−1⟩\langle 3,5,\dots,2n-1\rangle, which forces ℚ⁡(−15)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-15}) at the first level.

1. Introduction

The Jacobian Conjecture is false for n≥3n\geq 3 [4, 23]. In [21] the second author organized the graded case by the signature of the weight vector 𝐰\mathbf{w}, that is by its sign pattern: if 𝐰\mathbf{w} is elliptic then an equivariant Keller map is an automorphism, and for n=2n=2 no signature admits an equivariant counterexample. The present paper restricts to the three-dimensional unit-positive sector: primitive integral weights already written as 𝐰=(1,−r,−s),r,s≥1.\mathbf{w}=(1,-r,-s),\qquad r,s\geq 1. This is not every primitive hyperbolic weight; for example (2,−1,−1)(2,-1,-1) cannot be integrally rescaled to this form. Within the stated sector we prove nonemptiness for every weight and study orbits, invariants, braid classes, and fields of definition.

Fix a field KK of characteristic zero. We write 𝒦K​(n,𝐰)\mathcal{K}_{K}(n,\mathbf{w}) for the set of noninjective Keller self-maps of 𝔸Kn\mathbb{A}^{n}_{K} equivariant for 𝐰\mathbf{w}, and abbreviate 𝒦⁡(n,𝐰)=𝒦ℚ¯​(n,𝐰)\mathcal{K}(n,\mathbf{w})=\mathcal{K}_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(n,\mathbf{w}). We write 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} for the parameter scheme of [21, §8], and 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp} for the group of liftable automorphisms acting on it. Section 2 fixes these conventions, derives the master equation and the identity detJ​F=−κ\det JF=-\kappa relating the Keller constant to the determinant (Cor 2.4), and records that the monodromy of a graded map may be computed on its quotient cover (Lem 2.5).

Section 3 constructs the cyclic cone family of weight (1,−1,−1)(1,-1,-1). The construction takes a level k≥2k\geq 2 and a seed φ\varphi of degree dd, subject to two lift conditions, and returns a graded Keller map of generic fibre degree N=k​dN=kd. No seed of degree two satisfies the conditions (Cor 3.7), so d≥3d\geq 3; with that constraint every composite N≥6N\geq 6 is attained (Thm 3.11). The member of least degree produced this way is six-sheeted, defined over ℚ⁡(−15)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-15}), with threefold component degrees (15,27,3)(15,27,3) (Thm 3.19); there is a 3333-sheeted member over ℚ\mathbb{Q} with a rational collision (Thm 3.20). The complementary lower bound for this signature is the differential obstruction of [15, Cor. 1.5], which forces deg⁡A+deg⁡B+deg⁡Λ≥14\deg A+\deg B+\deg\Lambda\geq 14 for any member. No member descends to a two-variable Keller pair, and Prop 3.21 isolates the single coefficient responsible.

Section 4 constructs the beta–Hermite family. For every pair 2≤r≤s2\leq r\leq s it produces a map Fr,sF_{r,s} over a number field KrK_{r}, equivariant for source weights (1,−r,−s)(1,-r,-s) and target weights (−s,−r,1)(-s,-r,1), with detJ​Fr,s=−r\det JF_{r,s}=-r and generic fibre degree 2​r−12r-1 (Thm 4.2); the degrees of AA and BB are read off the degree of ρ\rho in Prop 4.4, and on the diagonal r=s=pr=s=p the class is 𝒴p,p,(p+2,2​p2−1,1)∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{p,p,(p+2,2p^{2}-1,1)}. Hence 𝒦⁡(3,(1,−r,−s))≠∅\mathcal{K}(3,(1,-r,-s))\neq\emptyset whenever 2≤r≤s2\leq r\leq s, and in particular for every repeated weight. The underlying one-variable cover is the beta polynomial family (Rem 4.7), so the new content is the graded realisation, not the cover type. The row r=2r=2 is rational, and for odd rr the field KrK_{r} is totally imaginary (Prop 4.5).

Section 5 separates orbits by invariants of the quotient cover. Left-right equivalence transports the finite normalization, the branch divisor, the inertia, the monodromy, and the branch and local value semigroups; these are intrinsic, whereas a passport or pole partition attached to a chosen pencil is not. The action of 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp} descends to left-right equivalence, so intrinsic invariants are orbit invariants (Lem 5.1). We exhibit an alternating shear member of degree twelve whose branch semigroup is ⟨6,26,27⟩\langle 6,26,27\rangle, while every cyclic member of degree twelve has 1111 in its branch semigroup. Since 11∉⟨6,26,27⟩11\notin\langle 6,26,27\rangle, the two are inequivalent under arbitrary polynomial left-right equivalence, and 𝒦⁡(3,(1,−1,−1))\mathcal{K}(3,(1,-1,-1)) carries at least two 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp}-orbits at generic degree twelve (Cor 5.8).

Section 6 computes the geometric monodromy of every member of both families, alternating or symmetric of full degree. Section 7 shows that at generic degree twelve there are infinitely many orbits: the normalised quartic seeds form a smooth plane cubic EE of pairwise distinct 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp}-orbits, and the forgetful map J:E→ℙ1J\colon E\to\mathbb{P}^{1} to unpointed quotient classes has degree six (Thm 7.9).

Section 8 resolves the flagship bounded scheme of weight (1,−1,−2)(1,-1,-2): assuming Hypothesis 8.4, its reduction is a single orbit of the bound-preserving gauge group (Thm 8.5), and puts its quotient cover in the cubic normal form used next. Section 9 propagates that cubic along the unit-weight boundary: for every s≥3s\geq 3 there is a rational member of weight (1,−1,−s)(1,-1,-s) with determinant −16-16, generic fibre degree three and monodromy S3S_{3} (Thm 9.2), which completes the three-dimensional unit-positive geography (Cor 9.5).

Section 10 treats the Nielsen classes, braid orbits, and arithmetic monodromy of the two families, and locates the alternating shear locus as a curve in the four-dimensional reduced Hurwitz space (Prop 10.16). Section 11 cuts that curve out exactly; assuming Hypothesis 11.3, it also identifies the normalised admissible-cover orbicurve and its rational intersection class (Theorems 11.1, 11.5 and 11.6). Section 12 determines the fields of definition through the second lift form, which diagonalises over ℚ\mathbb{Q} as ⟨3,5,…,2​n−1⟩\langle 3,5,\dots,2n-1\rangle (Thm 12.4).

2. Preliminaries

We keep the conventions of [21]. This section fixes notation and collects the facts used throughout.

2.1. Gradings and equivariant maps

Let KK be a field of characteristic zero. A weight vector 𝐰=(w1,…,wn)∈ℤn\mathbf{w}=(w_{1},\dots,w_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} with all wi≠0w_{i}\neq 0 defines an action of 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} on 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} by t⋅(x1,…,xn)=(tw1​x1,…,twn​xn)t\cdot(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=(t^{w_{1}}x_{1},\dots,t^{w_{n}}x_{n}), and a grading of K⁡[x1,…,xn]K[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] with wt⁡(xi)=wi\wt(x_{i})=w_{i}. The signature of 𝐰\mathbf{w} is the sign pattern of its entries, taken up to permutation and up to 𝐰↦−𝐰\mathbf{w}\mapsto-\mathbf{w}. We call 𝐰\mathbf{w} elliptic if all wiw_{i} have the same sign, and hyperbolic otherwise.

A polynomial map F:𝔸n→𝔸nF\colon\mathbb{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{A}^{n} is equivariant for source weights 𝐰\mathbf{w} and target weights 𝐰′\mathbf{w}^{\prime} if F⁡(t⋅p)=t∗F⁡(p)F(t\cdot p)=t\ast F(p), where ∗\ast is the action of 𝐰′\mathbf{w}^{\prime}. Equivalently, FiF_{i} is homogeneous of weight wi′w^{\prime}_{i} for the grading 𝐰\mathbf{w}. A Keller map is a polynomial map with detJ​F∈K×\det JF\in K^{\times}. We write 𝒦K​(n,𝐰)\mathcal{K}_{K}(n,\mathbf{w}) for the set of noninjective Keller self-maps of 𝔸Kn\mathbb{A}^{n}_{K} equivariant for 𝐰\mathbf{w}, and 𝒦⁡(n,𝐰)=𝒦ℚ¯​(n,𝐰)\mathcal{K}(n,\mathbf{w})=\mathcal{K}_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(n,\mathbf{w}). A collision is a pair of distinct points with the same image.

The generic fibre degree of a dominant FF is the degree of the field extension K⁡(x1,…,xn)/K⁡(F1,…,Fn)K(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})/K(F_{1},\dots,F_{n}), equivalently the number of preimages of a general point. A Keller map is noninjective if and only if this degree exceeds one.

2.2. Invariant coordinates and descent

From now on n=3n=3 and 𝐰=(1,−r,−s)\mathbf{w}=(1,-r,-s) with r,s≥1r,s\geq 1. Write the coordinates as x,y,zx,y,z, so wt⁡(x)=1\wt(x)=1, wt⁡(y)=−r\wt(y)=-r, wt⁡(z)=−s\wt(z)=-s. Put

u=xr​y,v=xs​z.u=x^{r}y,\qquad v=x^{s}z.

These are invariant, and K​[x,y,z]𝔾m=K⁡[u,v]K[x,y,z]^{\mathbb{G}_{m}}=K[u,v], since an invariant monomial xa​yb​zcx^{a}y^{b}z^{c} has a=r​b+s​ca=rb+sc and equals ub​vcu^{b}v^{c}.

Let FF be equivariant for source weights 𝐰\mathbf{w} and target weights (−s,−r,1)(-s,-r,1). Then xs​F1x^{s}F_{1}, xr​F2x^{r}F_{2} and x−1​F3x^{-1}F_{3} are invariant, so there are unique A,B,Λ∈K⁡[u,v]A,B,\Lambda\in K[u,v] with

(1) F=(A⁡(u,v)xs,B⁡(u,v)xr,x​Λ​(u,v)).F=\Bigl(\frac{A(u,v)}{x^{s}},\ \frac{B(u,v)}{x^{r}},\ x\Lambda(u,v)\Bigr).

We call (A,B,Λ)(A,B,\Lambda) the descended triple. The pairing is AA with ss and BB with rr; it is invisible when r=sr=s, and matters in the stratum 𝒴1,2,(4,3,1)∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{1,2,(4,3,1)}.

Lemma 2.1.

FF in Eq. 1 is polynomial if and only if every monomial ui​vju^{i}v^{j} occurring in AA satisfies r​i+s​j≥sri+sj\geq s, and every monomial occurring in BB satisfies r​i+s​j≥rri+sj\geq r. For r=sr=s both conditions read A,B∈(u,v)A,B\in(u,v), that is A⁡(0,0)=B⁡(0,0)=0A(0,0)=B(0,0)=0.

Proof.

ui​vj=xr​i+s​j​yi​zju^{i}v^{j}=x^{ri+sj}y^{i}z^{j}, so x−s​ui​vjx^{-s}u^{i}v^{j} is polynomial exactly when r​i+s​j≥sri+sj\geq s, and likewise for BB. ∎

We refer to the conditions of Lem 2.1 as the lift conditions, and to (u,v)=(0,0)(u,v)=(0,0) as the base point. For f,g∈K⁡[u,v]f,g\in K[u,v] write

(2) {f,g}=Jacu,v⁡(f,g)=fu​gv−fv​gu.\{f,g\}=\Jac_{u,v}(f,g)=f_{u}g_{v}-f_{v}g_{u}.

This bracket is antisymmetric and is a derivation in each argument. Set

(3) Q=Λs​A,P=Λr​B.Q=\Lambda^{s}A,\qquad P=\Lambda^{r}B.

These are the invariant coordinates of the target grading, namely Q=F1​F3sQ=F_{1}F_{3}^{\,s} and P=F2​F3rP=F_{2}F_{3}^{\,r}.

Lemma 2.2.

For A,B,Λ∈K⁡[u,v]A,B,\Lambda\in K[u,v] and integers r,s≥1r,s\geq 1,

Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)=Λr+s−1​(Λ⁡{B,A}+r​B​{Λ,A}+s​A​{B,Λ}).\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)=\Lambda^{r+s-1}\bigl(\Lambda\{B,A\}+rB\{\Lambda,A\}+sA\{B,\Lambda\}\bigr).
Proof.

Expanding Jacu,v⁡(Λr​B,Λs​A)\Jac_{u,v}(\Lambda^{r}B,\Lambda^{s}A) by the derivation property in each argument gives

Jacu,v⁡(Λr​B,Λs​A)=Λr​(Λs​{B,A}+A⁡{B,Λs})+B⁡(Λs​{Λr,A}+A⁡{Λr,Λs})=Λr+s​{B,A}+s​Λr+s−1​A​{B,Λ}+r​Λr+s−1​B​{Λ,A},\begin{split}\Jac_{u,v}(\Lambda^{r}B,\Lambda^{s}A)&=\Lambda^{r}\bigl(\Lambda^{s}\{B,A\}+A\{B,\Lambda^{s}\}\bigr)+B\bigl(\Lambda^{s}\{\Lambda^{r},A\}+A\{\Lambda^{r},\Lambda^{s}\}\bigr)\\ &=\Lambda^{r+s}\{B,A\}+s\Lambda^{r+s-1}A\{B,\Lambda\}+r\Lambda^{r+s-1}B\{\Lambda,A\},\end{split}

since {Λr,Λs}=0\{\Lambda^{r},\Lambda^{s}\}=0, {B,Λs}=s​Λs−1​{B,Λ}\{B,\Lambda^{s}\}=s\Lambda^{s-1}\{B,\Lambda\} and {Λr,A}=r​Λr−1​{Λ,A}\{\Lambda^{r},A\}=r\Lambda^{r-1}\{\Lambda,A\}. ∎

Proposition 2.3.

Let FF be as in Eq. 1 with Λ≠0\Lambda\neq 0. Then

detJ​F=−Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)Λr+s−1.\det JF=-\frac{\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)}{\Lambda^{r+s-1}}.

The substitution (x,y,z)↦(u,v,x)(x,y,z)\mapsto(u,v,x) has Jacobian determinant xr+sx^{r+s}, and (F1,F2,F3)↦(Q,P,F3)(F_{1},F_{2},F_{3})\mapsto(Q,P,F_{3}) has Jacobian determinant F3r+sF_{3}^{\,r+s}. Since Q,PQ,P depend only on u,vu,v and F3=x​ΛF_{3}=x\Lambda,

det∂(Q,P,F3)∂(u,v,x)=Λ​Jacu,v⁡(Q,P)=−Λ​Jacu,v⁡(P,Q).\det\frac{\partial(Q,P,F_{3})}{\partial(u,v,x)}=\Lambda\,\Jac_{u,v}(Q,P)=-\Lambda\,\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q).

The chain rule gives F3r+s​detJ​F=−Λ​Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)​xr+sF_{3}^{\,r+s}\det JF=-\Lambda\,\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)\,x^{r+s}, and F3=x​ΛF_{3}=x\Lambda. ∎

Corollary 2.4.

FF is Keller if and only if there is κ∈K×\kappa\in K^{\times} with

(4) Λ⁡{B,A}+r​B​{Λ,A}+s​A​{B,Λ}=κ,\Lambda\{B,A\}+rB\{\Lambda,A\}+sA\{B,\Lambda\}=\kappa,

and then detJ​F=−κ\det JF=-\kappa.

We call Eq. 4 the master equation and κ\kappa the Keller constant. A graded Keller map is thus the same thing as a triple (A,B,Λ)(A,B,\Lambda) satisfying Eq. 4 and the lift conditions of Lem 2.1.

Below we use the affine change (u,v)↦(Λ,v)(u,v)\mapsto(\Lambda,v) with Λ=1+u\Lambda=1+u, of Jacobian one, and take all brackets in (Λ,v)(\Lambda,v). Then {Λ,A}=Av\{\Lambda,A\}=A_{v} and {B,Λ}=−Bv\{B,\Lambda\}=-B_{v}, so Eq. 4 reads

(5) Λ⁡{B,A}+r​B​Av−s​A​Bv=κ.\Lambda\{B,A\}+rBA_{v}-sAB_{v}=\kappa.

In signature (1,−1,−1)(1,-1,-1) we write w=v−1w=v-1; brackets in (Λ,w)(\Lambda,w) agree with brackets in (Λ,v)(\Lambda,v). The base point (u,v)=(0,0)(u,v)=(0,0) becomes (Λ,v)=(1,0)(\Lambda,v)=(1,0), and (Λ,w)=(1,−1)(\Lambda,w)=(1,-1).

For 𝐝=(d1,d2,d3)\mathbf{d}=(d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}) let 𝒴r,s,𝐝\mathcal{Y}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} be the scheme of triples (A,B,Λ)(A,B,\Lambda) satisfying Eq. 4 and the lift conditions, with deg⁡A≤d1\deg A\leq d_{1}, deg⁡B≤d2\deg B\leq d_{2} and deg⁡Λ≤d3\deg\Lambda\leq d_{3}, all degrees in (u,v)(u,v). Let 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} be the open subscheme on which the three degrees are exactly d1,d2,d3d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}. Multiprojectivisation removes the three independent coefficient scalings. These are the schemes of [21].

We write 𝒢\mathcal{G} for the group of liftable automorphisms of [21, §8.5] and 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp} for the subgroup preserving the graded normal form. Two graded Keller maps are equivalent when they lie in one 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp}-orbit, and classification means the determination of these orbits.

2.3. The quotient cover

The pair (P,Q)(P,Q) of Eq. 3 is a polynomial self-map of 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} with Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)=κ​Λr+s−1\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)=\kappa\Lambda^{r+s-1}. We call it the quotient map of FF, and its normalization the quotient cover.

Lemma 2.5.

Let L=x​ΛL=x\Lambda. Then K⁡(x,y,z)=K⁡(u,v,L)K(x,y,z)=K(u,v,L) and K⁡(F1,F2,F3)=K⁡(P,Q,L)K(F_{1},F_{2},F_{3})=K(P,Q,L), and LL is transcendental over K⁡(u,v)K(u,v). Hence the generic fibre degree of FF equals [K(u,v):K(P,Q)][K(u,v):K(P,Q)].

Proof.

x=L/Λx=L/\Lambda recovers xx from u,v,Lu,v,L, and y,zy,z follow from u=xr​yu=x^{r}y, v=xs​zv=x^{s}z. On the target, F3=LF_{3}=L, F1=Q/LsF_{1}=Q/L^{s} and F2=P/LrF_{2}=P/L^{r}. The extension K⁡(u,v,L)/K⁡(P,Q,L)K(u,v,L)/K(P,Q,L) is the purely transcendental base change of K⁡(u,v)/K⁡(P,Q)K(u,v)/K(P,Q) along K⁡(P,Q,L)/K⁡(P,Q)K(P,Q,L)/K(P,Q), so the degree is unchanged. ∎

We write NN for this degree and call it the generic fibre degree of the member. By Lem 2.5 the normal closure group of FF over its target function field equals that of the quotient cover, so all monodromy statements may be made downstairs.

Fixing the second target coordinate at a general value YY cuts the quotient cover down to a degree-NN cover of curves. The passport of that cover is the list of its inertia cycle types, and the pole partition is the cycle type over the point at infinity. Both depend on the choice of second coordinate.

2.4. Branch curves and semigroups

Let f=(P,Q)f=(P,Q) be the quotient map, dominant of degree NN, and let Γf⊂𝔸2\Gamma_{f}\subset\mathbb{A}^{2} be the union of the one-dimensional components of the locus over which the fibre has fewer than NN points, taken with its reduced structure. We call Γf\Gamma_{f} the branch curve of ff. It is not the image of the critical locus {Jacu,v(P,Q)=0}\{\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)=0\}: by Cor 2.4 that locus is {Λ=0}\{\Lambda=0\}, and Q=Λs​AQ=\Lambda^{s}A and P=Λr​BP=\Lambda^{r}B both vanish there, so it is contracted to the origin and every component of Γf\Gamma_{f} records a failure of properness rather than a critical value.

Let Γ\Gamma be an irreducible component of Γf\Gamma_{f}, with affine coordinate ring ℂ⁡[Γ]\mathbb{C}[\Gamma] and normalisation Γ~\widetilde{\Gamma}. A place at infinity of Γ\Gamma is a place of Γ~\widetilde{\Gamma} at which some element of ℂ⁡[Γ]\mathbb{C}[\Gamma] has a pole. Suppose Γ\Gamma has exactly one, as does every branch curve occurring below, and write ν\nu for the valuation there. The semigroup at infinity of Γ\Gamma is

S∞​(Γ)={−ν⁡(g):g∈ℂ⁡[Γ]∖{0}}⊂ℤ≥0.S_{\infty}(\Gamma)=\{-\nu(g)\ :\ g\in\mathbb{C}[\Gamma]\setminus\{0\}\}\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

All the branch curves below are given by a birational parametrisation t↦(g1​(t),…,gm​(t))t\mapsto\bigl(g_{1}(t),\dots,g_{m}(t)\bigr) with gi∈ℂ⁡[t]g_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[t]. Then Γ~=𝔸t1\widetilde{\Gamma}=\mathbb{A}^{1}_{t}, the place at infinity is unique, ℂ⁡[Γ]=ℂ⁡[g1,…,gm]\mathbb{C}[\Gamma]=\mathbb{C}[g_{1},\dots,g_{m}] and ν=−deg\nu=-\deg, so S∞​(Γ)S_{\infty}(\Gamma) is the set of degrees of the nonzero elements of ℂ⁡[g1,…,gm]\mathbb{C}[g_{1},\dots,g_{m}]. Since degrees add under multiplication, this set contains the numerical semigroup ⟨deg⁡g1,…,deg⁡gm⟩\langle\deg g_{1},\dots,\deg g_{m}\rangle. The containment can be strict: two monomials in the gig_{i} of equal degree may have cancelling leading terms, and the resulting difference has a degree that need not lie in the semigroup generated by the deg⁡gi\deg g_{i}. This occurs, for instance, when deg⁡g1=6\deg g_{1}=6 and deg⁡g2=27\deg g_{2}=27: the relation 2⋅27=9⋅62\cdot 27=9\cdot 6 forces a cancellation producing degree 26∉⟨6,27⟩26\notin\langle 6,27\rangle. The following criterion is what rules out any further such degree.

Lemma 2.6.

Let g1,…,gm∈ℂ⁡[t]g_{1},\dots,g_{m}\in\mathbb{C}[t] be monic of degrees d1,…,dmd_{1},\dots,d_{m}, and let

I𝐝=ker(ℂ[x1,…,xm]⟶ℂ[t],xi⟼tdi)I_{\mathbf{d}}=\ker\bigl(\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}]\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}[t],\quad x_{i}\longmapsto t^{d_{i}}\bigr)

be the toric ideal of the numerical semigroup ⟨d1,…,dm⟩\langle d_{1},\dots,d_{m}\rangle. For u∈ℤ≥0mu\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{m} write gu=g1u1⋯gmumg^{u}=g_{1}^{u_{1}}\cdots g_{m}^{u_{m}}. Suppose I𝐝I_{\mathbf{d}} is generated by homogeneous binomials xuj−xvjx^{u_{j}}-x^{v_{j}}, 1≤j≤q1\leq j\leq q, and that for each jj the corresponding difference guj−gvjg^{u_{j}}-g^{v_{j}} can be written as a polynomial in the gig_{i} all of whose monomials have weighted degree strictly smaller than ∑i(uj)i​di=∑i(vj)i​di\sum_{i}(u_{j})_{i}d_{i}=\sum_{i}(v_{j})_{i}d_{i}. Then the degrees of the nonzero elements of ℂ⁡[g1,…,gm]\mathbb{C}[g_{1},\dots,g_{m}] are exactly ⟨d1,…,dm⟩\langle d_{1},\dots,d_{m}\rangle.

Proof.

One containment is immediate. For the other, write an element of the subalgebra as a polynomial in the gig_{i} and choose an expression for which the largest weighted degree DD is minimal. If the actual degree is smaller than DD, the sum of the terms of weight DD is a homogeneous relation among td1,…,tdmt^{d_{1}},\dots,t^{d_{m}}, hence lies in the degree-DD part of the toric ideal I𝐝I_{\mathbf{d}}. Express that relation using the stated homogeneous binomial generators. Replacing each generator guj−gvjg^{u_{j}}-g^{v_{j}} by its lower-weight expression lowers the largest weight of the chosen representation, a contradiction. Therefore the actual degree equals DD, which belongs to the numerical semigroup. ∎

Remark 2.7.

Lemma 2.6 is the subalgebra form of a leading-term argument. For an ideal, a Gröbner basis is a generating set whose leading terms generate the ideal of all leading terms, and Buchberger’s criterion tests this on the syzygies between leading terms. Here the object controlled is the subalgebra ℂ⁡[g1,…,gm]\mathbb{C}[g_{1},\dots,g_{m}] rather than an ideal, the role of the ideal of leading terms is played by the algebra generated by td1,…,tdmt^{d_{1}},\dots,t^{d_{m}}, and the relations to be tested are the additive ones among the did_{i}, that is the toric ideal of the numerical semigroup. The general theory is developed in [19]; for the two computations below only the criterion above is needed, and in both the toric ideal has a single or a pair of explicit binomial generators.

Lemma 2.8.

Let f2=ψ∘f1∘ϕ−1f_{2}=\psi\circ f_{1}\circ\phi^{-1} with ϕ,ψ\phi,\psi polynomial automorphisms of 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}. Then ψ\psi carries Γf1\Gamma_{f_{1}} isomorphically onto Γf2\Gamma_{f_{2}}, and the multiset of semigroups at infinity of the components is the same for both. In particular S∞S_{\infty} is an invariant of the left–right equivalence class.

Proof.

Since ϕ\phi and ψ\psi are bijective, #​f2−1​(ψ⁡(y))=#​f1−1​(y)\#f_{2}^{-1}(\psi(y))=\#f_{1}^{-1}(y) for every yy, so ψ⁡(Γf1)=Γf2\psi(\Gamma_{f_{1}})=\Gamma_{f_{2}} and ψ\psi restricts to an isomorphism of reduced affine curves. Such an isomorphism carries coordinate rings to coordinate rings, hence normalisations to normalisations and places at infinity to places at infinity, and preserves valuations. ∎

A passport or a pole partition, by contrast, is attached to a chosen second coordinate and is invariant only under equivalences preserving that pencil. This is the distinction between intrinsic and framed data.

Theorem 3.11.

Proposition 3.12.

deg⁡Mφ=k⁡(d−2),Mφ​(0)=(−1)k+1​c2k2​k−1≠0,[Wk⁡(d−2)]​Mφ=(−1)k+1​cdkk​d−1.\begin{split}\deg M_{\varphi}&=k(d-2),\\ M_{\varphi}(0)&=\frac{(-1)^{k+1}c_{2}^{\,k}}{2k-1}\neq 0,\\ [W^{k(d-2)}]\,M_{\varphi}&=\frac{(-1)^{k+1}c_{d}^{\,k}}{kd-1}.\end{split}

We call MφM_{\varphi} the marking polynomial of φ\varphi, and its roots the admissible markings. There are k⁡(d−2)k(d-2) of them counted with multiplicity, none at the origin, and by Prop 3.12 a seed satisfies the second lift condition exactly when ϵ\epsilon is one of them. Lemma 3.15.

Let n=d−2≥1n=d-2\geq 1 and φ0=W2+Wd\varphi_{0}=W^{2}+W^{d}. Then

Corollary 3.16.

For every k≥2k\geq 2 and d≥3d\geq 3 there is a nonempty open locus of seeds of degree dd on which the marking polynomial is separable and the rescaling stabilizer is trivial. On that locus a seed carries exactly k⁡(d−2)k(d-2) admissible markings, and the k⁡(d−2)k(d-2) normalised seeds φw\varphi_{w} are pairwise distinct.

Proof.

On cd≠0c_{d}\neq 0 the coefficients of MφM_{\varphi} are polynomial in (c2,…,cd)(c_{2},\dots,c_{d}) of constant degree k⁡(d−2)k(d-2) by Prop 3.12, so separability is the nonvanishing of a discriminant and is open; it is nonempty by Lem 3.15. Triviality of the stabilizer holds on the open locus c2​c3≠0c_{2}c_{3}\neq 0 by Prop 3.14, which is nonempty. The space of seeds of degree dd is irreducible, so the two open loci meet. The count is Prop 3.12 and Prop 3.14. ∎

Lemma 3.17.

For every k≥2k\geq 2 and d≥3d\geq 3 the normalised seeds of degree dd satisfying Eq. 10 form a locally closed subscheme of the affine space of coefficients (c2,…,cd)(c_{2},\dots,c_{d}), pure of dimension d−3d-3 and nonempty. At d=3d=3 it is a finite set of points, and at d=4d=4 an affine plane curve.

Proof.

The two conditions of Eq. 10 cut the locus, so every component has dimension at least d−3d-3. For the upper bound, the first condition φ⁡(ϵ)=1\varphi(\epsilon)=1 is a nontrivial affine-linear equation, hence defines an irreducible affine hyperplane HH of dimension d−2d-2. The restriction of the second lift form to HH is not identically zero: the seed φ=W2\varphi=W^{2} lies on HH and

𝒬(k)​(W2)=∫0ϵW2​k−2​𝑑W=ϵ2​k−1≠0,\mathcal{Q}^{(k)}(W^{2})=\int_{0}^{\epsilon}W^{2k-2}\,dW=\frac{\epsilon}{2k-1}\neq 0,

using ϵ2​k−1=ϵ\epsilon^{2k-1}=\epsilon. Its zero scheme in HH is therefore an effective Cartier divisor, so every component has dimension exactly d−3d-3. The exact-degree locus cd≠0c_{d}\neq 0 is open in it and nonempty by Thm 3.11, which supplies a seed of exact degree dd at every level. ∎

Theorem 3.18.

Let k≥2k\geq 2 and d≥3d\geq 3. On the open locus of Cor 3.16, forgetting the admissible marking is finite étale of degree k⁡(d−2)k(d-2) from normalised seeds to rescaling classes of seeds. In general its coarse fibre over φ\varphi is the set of nonzero roots of MφM_{\varphi} modulo the finite rescaling stabilizer. The normalised exact-degree seed locus has dimension d−3d-3 and maps to

𝒴1,1,((2​k−1)​d−1,(2​k−1)​(k​d−1)−1, 1)∘.\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{1,1,((2k-1)d-1,\,(2k-1)(kd-1)-1,\,1)}.

Within a fixed regular rescaling class, its k⁡(d−2)k(d-2) normalised representatives are pairwise distinct as normalised seeds. No graded-orbit separation claim is made here; the quartic case is treated separately in Thm 7.9.

Proof.

A simple admissible marking ww determines the normalised seed φw\varphi_{w} by Prop 3.14. On the open locus of Cor 3.16 the k⁡(d−2)k(d-2) markings are simple and the stabilizer is trivial, so the count is exact and discriminant nonvanishing makes the map étale. The covariance Lem 3.13 gives the coarse statement in general. The dimension and degree box are Lemmas 3.17 and 3.8. The pairwise distinctness of the normalised representatives follows from the trivial stabilizer in Prop 3.14. ∎

Proposition 3.21.

Under T=Λ​wT=\Lambda w one has Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)=Λ​JacΛ,T⁡(P^,Q^)\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)=\Lambda\Jac_{\Lambda,T}(\widehat{P},\widehat{Q}), so (P^,Q^)(\widehat{P},\widehat{Q}) has Jacobian one. Finally W=Tk/ΛW=T^{k}/\Lambda, so φ⁡(W)=∑jcj​Tk​j​Λ−j\varphi(W)=\sum_{j}c_{j}T^{kj}\Lambda^{-j} and the top term is cd​Tk​d​Λ−dc_{d}T^{kd}\Lambda^{-d} with cd≠0c_{d}\neq 0. ∎

Proposition 3.22.

Fix a generic value YY of QQ. Remark 4.6.

The field of Prop 4.5(2) coincides with the field of Thm 3.19. In the cyclic family that field is forced by the second lift condition; here it arises from the factorisation of M3M_{3}, and nothing so far connects the two.

Remark 4.7.

At fixed QQ one has ∂P/∂ρ∝(ρ2−1−2​Q)r−1\partial P/\partial\rho\propto(\rho^{2}-1-2Q)^{r-1}, whose two roots are distinct for generic QQ. After an affine change carrying them to 00 and 11 this is proportional to ξr−1​(1−ξ)r−1\xi^{r-1}(1-\xi)^{r-1}, so the generic quotient cover is the beta polynomial cover of degree 2​r−12r-1, with two finite branch points of cycle type (r,1r−1)(r,1^{r-1}) and a full (2​r−1)(2r-1)-cycle at infinity. The content of Thm 4.2 is therefore the graded realisation, in the sense of [21, Rem. 8.13], and not a new class of one-variable cover.

4.1. Rooted quotient reconstruction

Fix p≥1p\geq 1 and the repeated weight 𝐰=(1,−p,−p)\mathbf{w}=(1,-p,-p); the case p=1p=1 is the balanced signature of Sec. 3. The quotient map of a graded Keller map with triple (A,B,Λ)(A,B,\Lambda) is

f=(P,Q)=(B​Λp,A​Λp):𝔸2⟶𝔸2,f=(P,Q)=(B\Lambda^{p},\ A\Lambda^{p})\colon\mathbb{A}^{2}\longrightarrow\mathbb{A}^{2},

(20) {P,Q}=Λ2​p−1​(Λ⁡{B,A}+p​B​{Λ,A}+p​A​{B,Λ})=κ​Λ2​p−1.\{P,Q\}=\Lambda^{2p-1}\bigl(\Lambda\{B,A\}+pB\{\Lambda,A\}+pA\{B,\Lambda\}\bigr)=\kappa\Lambda^{2p-1}.

Let oo be the distinguished invariant source point above the target origin. The lift conditions give A⁡(o)=B⁡(o)=0A(o)=B(o)=0 and Λ⁡(o)≠0\Lambda(o)\neq 0, so f⁡(o)=0f(o)=0 and oo is unramified.

A pointed polynomial map (f,o)(f,o), f=(P,Q)f=(P,Q), is pp-admissible if f⁡(o)=0f(o)=0, {P,Q}​(o)≠0\{P,Q\}(o)\neq 0, and there is a polynomial λf\lambda_{f}, normalised by λf​(o)=1\lambda_{f}(o)=1, with

{P,Q}{P,Q}​(o)=λf2​p−1,λfp∣P,λfp∣Q.\frac{\{P,Q\}}{\{P,Q\}(o)}=\lambda_{f}^{2p-1},\qquad\lambda_{f}^{p}\mid P,\qquad\lambda_{f}^{p}\mid Q.

For p≥1p\geq 1 write

𝒳p={graded Keller maps of weight ​(1,−p,−p)}/𝒢♯,𝒫p={p-admissible pointed maps}/pointed left–right equivalence.\begin{split}\mathcal{X}_{p}&=\{\text{graded Keller maps of weight }(1,-p,-p)\}/\mathcal{G}^{\sharp},\\ \mathcal{P}_{p}&=\{\text{$p$-admissible pointed maps}\}/\text{pointed left--right equivalence}.\end{split}
Theorem 4.9.

The quotient construction induces a bijection

𝒳p→∼𝒫p,\mathcal{X}_{p}\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;\mathcal{P}_{p},

whose inverse reconstructs the coefficient classes

[A]=[Q/λfp],[B]=[P/λfp],[Λ]=[λf].[A]=\bigl[Q/\lambda_{f}^{p}\bigr],\qquad[B]=\bigl[P/\lambda_{f}^{p}\bigr],\qquad[\Lambda]=[\lambda_{f}].

Every pointed left–right equivalence of quotient maps lifts to a graded equivalence, uniquely up to the universal grading torus.

Proof.

Evaluating Eq. 20 at oo and dividing gives {P,Q}/{P,Q}​(o)=(Λ/Λ⁡(o))2​p−1\{P,Q\}/\{P,Q\}(o)=(\Lambda/\Lambda(o))^{2p-1}; in characteristic zero a polynomial (2​p−1)(2p-1)-th root normalised at oo is unique, so λf=Λ/Λ⁡(o)\lambda_{f}=\Lambda/\Lambda(o), and division recovers the three classes. This proves pp-admissibility of the quotient and the reconstruction formula; in particular the assignment 𝒳p→𝒫p\mathcal{X}_{p}\to\mathcal{P}_{p} is defined and, by reconstruction, surjective.

Suppose f2∘σ=τ∘f1f_{2}\circ\sigma=\tau\circ f_{1} with σ⁡(o1)=o2\sigma(o_{1})=o_{2} and τ⁡(0)=0\tau(0)=0. Plane polynomial automorphisms have constant Jacobian, so dividing the transformation law ({P2,Q2}∘σ)​cσ=cτ​{P1,Q1}(\{P_{2},Q_{2}\}\circ\sigma)\,c_{\sigma}=c_{\tau}\,\{P_{1},Q_{1}\} by its value at o1o_{1} gives λf2∘σ=λf1\lambda_{f_{2}}\circ\sigma=\lambda_{f_{1}}, both sides being the normalised root. Hence a pointed equivalence carries the reconstructed triple of f1f_{1} to that of f2f_{2} along (σ,τ)(\sigma,\tau).

Injectivity therefore reduces to lifting (σ,τ)(\sigma,\tau) to a graded equivalence. In the invariant coordinates u=xp​yu=x^{p}y, v=xp​zv=x^{p}z, an origin-fixing source automorphism σ=(σ1,σ2)\sigma=(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}) lifts, for any a∈𝔾ma\in\mathbb{G}_{m}, to

(x,y,z)⟼(a​x,σ1​(xp​y,xp​z)ap​xp,σ2​(xp​y,xp​z)ap​xp),(x,y,z)\longmapsto\Bigl(ax,\ \frac{\sigma_{1}(x^{p}y,x^{p}z)}{a^{p}x^{p}},\ \frac{\sigma_{2}(x^{p}y,x^{p}z)}{a^{p}x^{p}}\Bigr),

which is polynomial because every monomial of σi\sigma_{i} has positive total degree, and which induces σ\sigma on (u,v)(u,v). The analogous formula lifts an origin-fixing target automorphism. Choosing the same scalar aa in both lifts makes the weight-one coordinates agree, and the identities P=B​ΛpP=B\Lambda^{p}, Q=A​ΛpQ=A\Lambda^{p} then give equality of the remaining components. The residual scalar is the universal grading torus, and the converse descent is immediate. ∎

Remark 4.10.

Equivalently, for a graded Keller map FF with pointed quotient (f,o)(f,o) there is an exact sequence

1⟶𝔾m⟶Aut𝒢♯⁡(F)⟶Aut⁡(f,o)⟶1,1\longrightarrow\mathbb{G}_{m}\longrightarrow\Aut_{\mathcal{G}^{\sharp}}(F)\longrightarrow\Aut(f,o)\longrightarrow 1,

where Aut⁡(f,o)\Aut(f,o) is the group of pointed left–right self-equivalences of ff. Surjectivity is the lifting statement, and the kernel consists of the graded automorphisms inducing the identity on the quotient, that is the universal grading torus.

Remark 4.11.

For unequal weights (1,−r,−s)(1,-r,-s) the identity Eq. 20 holds with exponent r+s−1r+s-1, and the normalised root λf\lambda_{f} still exists. Full lifting is special to r=sr=s: the two divisibility conditions become λfr|P\lambda_{f}^{r}\mid P and λfs|Q\lambda_{f}^{s}\mid Q, and an arbitrary quotient automorphism need not preserve them.

5. Orbit separation by quotient invariants

Left-right equivalence of quotient maps transports the finite normalization, the branch divisor, the inertia, the monodromy, and the affine branch algebras with their normalization valuations, hence also the branch and local value semigroups of Sec. 2.4. These are intrinsic invariants. A passport or pole partition attached to a chosen pencil is framed data, invariant only under equivalences preserving the pencil. Finally, the graded map retains the lift-point marking above the quotient origin, which is pointed data not visible on the quotient cover at all. This section uses the first level only, and shows that it already separates two orbits at generic degree twelve.

Lemma 5.1.

If two graded Keller maps lie in one 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp}-orbit, their quotient maps are polynomially left-right equivalent. Consequently every intrinsic invariant of the quotient map is constant on 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp}-orbits.

Proof.

By [21, §8.5] an element of 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp} acts by F↦Ψ∘F∘Φ−1F\mapsto\Psi\circ F\circ\Phi^{-1} with Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi graded automorphisms of 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3} for the source and target weights. Each preserves the 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-action, hence descends to an automorphism of the invariant plane: Φ\Phi to ϕ\phi in the coordinates (u,v)(u,v), and Ψ\Psi to ψ\psi in the coordinates (P,Q)(P,Q) of Eq. 3. Since (P,Q)(P,Q) is the restriction of FF to invariants, the quotient map of Ψ∘F∘Φ−1\Psi\circ F\circ\Phi^{-1} is ψ∘(P,Q)∘ϕ−1\psi\circ(P,Q)\circ\phi^{-1}, which is left-right equivalent to (P,Q)(P,Q). ∎

The converse fails, and by a definite amount.

Theorem 5.5.

P⁡(X,Y)P(X,Y) is indecomposable over the algebraic closure of ℂ⁡(Y)\mathbb{C}(Y), and its geometric monodromy group is A12A_{12}.

Proof.

Suppose P=g∘hP=g\circ h with deg⁡g=a>1\deg g=a>1, deg⁡h=b>1\deg h=b>1, a​b=12ab=12. Every finite ramification index of PP is three by Thm 5.4.

Suppose gg has one pole. After a fractional linear change gg is a polynomial, totally ramified over infinity, so each pole of PP has index divisible by aa; thus aa divides 33 and 99, forcing a=3a=3, b=4b=4. If the two critical points of the cubic gg were distinct, each would be simple, and a point of h−1h^{-1} above such a critical value would have index 2​eh2e_{h} in PP, which is even and at least two, hence never three. So the critical points coincide and gg is conjugate to z3+constz^{3}+\mathrm{const}. Its finite critical point has four preimages under hh counted with multiplicity; any with eh>1e_{h}>1 would give index 3​eh>33e_{h}>3, so all four are unramified and give four points of index three over a single critical value, that is cycle type (3,3,3,3)(3,3,3,3), contradicting Thm 5.4.

Suppose instead gg has two poles. Then PP has two poles, so each pole of gg has a unique hh-preimage and hh is totally ramified there; hence bb divides 33 and 99, forcing b=3b=3, a=4a=4. A degree-three rational function totally ramified at two points is conjugate to X3X^{3}, so P∈ℂ​(Y)​(X3)P\in\mathbb{C}(Y)(X^{3}). But the coefficient of XX in Eq. 23 is

1+6​c​d​Y2+15​c2​d2​Y4,1+6cdY^{2}+15c^{2}d^{2}Y^{4},

not identically zero.

Both arguments use only pole orders, the distinctness of the six finite critical values, and one coefficient, all preserved by base change to the algebraic closure. So the cover is indecomposable and its monodromy is primitive. A finite inertia generator is a three-cycle, so A12≤MonA_{12}\leq\mathrm{Mon} by Jordan’s theorem. Every inertia generator is even, the finite ones being three-cycles and the one at infinity of type (9,3)(9,3), so Mon≤A12\mathrm{Mon}\leq A_{12}. ∎

Corollary 5.8.

The degree-twelve alternating shear quotient is not left–right equivalent to the quotient of any member of Sec. 3 of generic degree twelve. Hence 𝒦⁡(3,(1,−1,−1))\mathcal{K}(3,(1,-1,-1)) carries at least two 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp}-orbits at generic degree twelve.

Proof.

Let N=k​d=12N=kd=12 with k≥2k\geq 2 and d≥3d\geq 3. Then (k,d)∈{(2,6),(3,4),(4,3)}(k,d)\in\{(2,6),(3,4),(4,3)\}, and all three occur by Thm 3.11. By Prop 3.22, the cyclic branch curve is the union of the line {Q=0}\{Q=0\} and the component parametrised by (A0​(W),φ​(W))(A_{0}(W),\varphi(W)), of degrees 1111 and dd. Since gcd⁡(11,d)=1\gcd(11,d)=1, this parametrisation is birational, so the non-line component has 1111 in its semigroup at infinity.

The line is intrinsically distinguished as the unique component whose semigroup at infinity is ℤ≥0\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. Indeed, for the cyclic non-line component both parametrising coordinates have order at least two at W=0W=0 (φ∈W2​ℂ​[W]\varphi\in W^{2}\mathbb{C}[W] and ord0⁡A0≥2​k−1\operatorname{ord}_{0}A_{0}\geq 2k-1), so its affine coordinate ring is not ℂ⁡[W]\mathbb{C}[W]. If its semigroup contained 11, it would contain a degree-one polynomial in WW, forcing that coordinate ring to equal ℂ⁡[W]\mathbb{C}[W], a contradiction. The alternating-shear non-line component has semigroup ⟨6,26,27⟩\langle 6,26,27\rangle by Thm 5.7, and likewise does not contain 11.

A left–right equivalence must therefore match the two line components and the two non-line components. The cyclic non-line semigroup contains 1111, whereas 11∉⟨6,26,27⟩11\notin\langle 6,26,27\rangle. The quotients are not left–right equivalent by Lem 2.8, and Lem 5.1 separates the graded orbits. ∎

Remark 5.9.

The separation in Cor 5.8 uses no choice of pencil: it compares the intrinsic branch semigroups directly, and so holds under arbitrary polynomial left-right equivalence of the quotients. This answers the fibration question raised by the framed passports (9,3)(9,3) and (11,1)(11,1), which by themselves are invariant only under equivalences preserving the pencil.

6. Monodromy of the two families

We determine the geometric monodromy group of the generic quotient cover of every member of both families. Throughout, the cover means the degree-NN extension at a generic value of the pencil, and inertia generators are taken at the branch points of Prop 3.22, Rem 4.7 or Thm 5.4 as appropriate.

We use three standard facts about primitive groups. A transitive subgroup of SnS_{n} containing a cycle with exactly one fixed point is 22-transitive, since the stabilizer of that point contains an (n−1)(n-1)-cycle on the remaining points. A primitive subgroup of SnS_{n} containing a 33-cycle contains AnA_{n}, by Jordan’s theorem. A primitive subgroup of SnS_{n} containing a cycle with at least three fixed points contains AnA_{n}. A cover with primitive monodromy group is indecomposable.

Theorem 6.1.

Let Π\Pi be the quotient cover of a member of Sec. 3 with parameters (k,d)(k,d), so k≥2k\geq 2, d≥3d\geq 3 and N=k​d≥6N=kd\geq 6. Then Π\Pi is indecomposable, and its geometric monodromy group is

Mon⁡(Π)={AN,k​ even,SN,k​ odd.\mathrm{Mon}(\Pi)=\begin{cases}A_{N},&k\text{ even},\\ S_{N},&k\text{ odd}.\end{cases}
Proof.

Fix a generic value YY of the pencil. By Prop 3.22 the pole partition is (N−1,1)(N-1,1), so an inertia generator at infinity is an (N−1)(N-1)-cycle fixing exactly one point. Hence the monodromy is 22-transitive, in particular primitive, and Π\Pi is indecomposable.

By Lem 3.4 the finite critical points are the roots of φ⁡(W)=Y\varphi(W)=Y, which are dd in number and simple for generic YY, each of local degree k+1k+1. The associated branch values are the points A0​(Wi)A_{0}(W_{i}). Since deg⁡A0=N−1\deg A_{0}=N-1 and deg⁡φ=d\deg\varphi=d by Prop 3.6, and [ℂ(W):ℂ(A0,φ)][\mathbb{C}(W):\mathbb{C}(A_{0},\varphi)] divides both, it divides gcd⁡(k​d−1,d)=1\gcd(kd-1,d)=1; so W↦(A0​(W),φ⁡(W))W\mapsto\bigl(A_{0}(W),\varphi(W)\bigr) is birational and the dd branch values are distinct for generic YY. Each finite inertia generator is therefore a (k+1)(k+1)-cycle, and Riemann–Hurwitz is exact:

d⁡((k+1)−1)+(N−1−1)=k​d+N−2=2​N−2.d\bigl((k+1)-1\bigr)+(N-1-1)=kd+N-2=2N-2.

A finite inertia generator fixes N−k−1=k⁡(d−1)−1N-k-1=k(d-1)-1 points, and k≥2k\geq 2, d≥3d\geq 3 give k⁡(d−1)−1≥3k(d-1)-1\geq 3. By [16] AN≤Mon⁡(Π)A_{N}\leq\mathrm{Mon}(\Pi).

Parity decides the rest. A (k+1)(k+1)-cycle is even if and only if kk is even, and the (N−1)(N-1)-cycle is even if and only if NN is even. If kk is even then N=k​dN=kd is even and every inertia generator is even, so Mon⁡(Π)≤AN\mathrm{Mon}(\Pi)\leq A_{N} and equality holds. If kk is odd the finite generators are odd, so Mon⁡(Π)≰AN\mathrm{Mon}(\Pi)\not\leq A_{N} and Mon⁡(Π)=SN\mathrm{Mon}(\Pi)=S_{N}. ∎

Remark 6.2.

The signs are consistent with the relation that the product of all inertia generators is trivial: the dd finite generators contribute (−1)k​d(-1)^{kd} in total and the generator at infinity contributes (−1)N(-1)^{N}, and N=k​dN=kd.

Lemma 6.3.

A polynomial of degree at least two with exactly two distinct finite critical points is indecomposable.

Proof.

Let ff have degree nn and finite critical points {W1,W2}\{W_{1},W_{2}\}, and suppose f=g∘hf=g\circ h with g,h∈ℂ⁡(z)g,h\in\mathbb{C}(z) of degrees a,b>1a,b>1. Since f−1​(∞)={∞}f^{-1}(\infty)=\{\infty\} and f−1​(∞)=h−1​(g−1​(∞))f^{-1}(\infty)=h^{-1}\bigl(g^{-1}(\infty)\bigr), the set g−1​(∞)g^{-1}(\infty) is the single point h⁡(∞)h(\infty). Replacing gg by g∘μg\circ\mu and hh by μ−1∘h\mu^{-1}\circ h for a Möbius map μ\mu carrying ∞\infty to h⁡(∞)h(\infty), we may assume gg and hh are polynomials. Each is then totally ramified at infinity, so by Riemann–Hurwitz the finite ramification of hh is b−1b-1 and that of gg is a−1a-1.

If WW is a finite critical point of hh then ef​(W)=eh​(W)​eg​(h⁡(W))>1e_{f}(W)=e_{h}(W)\,e_{g}(h(W))>1, so W∈{W1,W2}W\in\{W_{1},W_{2}\}; and if η\eta is a finite critical point of gg then every point of h−1​(η)h^{-1}(\eta) is a critical point of ff, so h−1​(η)⊆{W1,W2}h^{-1}(\eta)\subseteq\{W_{1},W_{2}\}. Since a−1≥1a-1\geq 1, the polynomial gg has at least one finite critical point. Let η1,…,ηm\eta_{1},\dots,\eta_{m} be its distinct finite critical points; the sets h−1​(ηj)h^{-1}(\eta_{j}) are nonempty and pairwise disjoint inside a set of two elements, so m≤2m\leq 2.

If m=2m=2 then each h−1​(ηj)h^{-1}(\eta_{j}) is a single point, at which hh is totally ramified, contributing b−1b-1 to the finite ramification of hh; two such contributions give 2​(b−1)>b−12(b-1)>b-1, which is impossible.

If m=1m=1 and h−1​(η1)h^{-1}(\eta_{1}) is a single point W0W_{0}, then hh is totally ramified there and its finite ramification b−1b-1 is exhausted, so W0W_{0} is the only finite critical point of hh. Then the finite critical points of ff are {W0}∪h−1​(η1)={W0}\{W_{0}\}\cup h^{-1}(\eta_{1})=\{W_{0}\}, contradicting that there are two.

If m=1m=1 and h−1​(η1)h^{-1}(\eta_{1}) has two points, then h−1​(η1)={W1,W2}h^{-1}(\eta_{1})=\{W_{1},W_{2}\}, and the ramification of hh over η1\eta_{1} is b−2b-2. Every finite critical point of hh lies in {W1,W2}\{W_{1},W_{2}\}, so this is all of the finite ramification of hh, giving b−2=b−1b-2=b-1.

All three cases are impossible, so no such decomposition exists. ∎

Corollary 6.4.

For p≥2p\geq 2 the beta polynomial βp\beta_{p} is indecomposable.

Proof.

By Rem 4.7 the derivative of βp\beta_{p} is proportional to ξp−1​(1−ξ)p−1\xi^{p-1}(1-\xi)^{p-1}, so βp\beta_{p} has exactly the two finite critical points 00 and 11. Apply Lem 6.3. ∎

Theorem 6.5.

The geometric monodromy group of the generic quotient cover of Fr,sF_{r,s} is A2​r−1A_{2r-1} for rr odd and S2​r−1S_{2r-1} for rr even.

Proof.

By Rem 4.7 the cover has degree 2​r−12r-1, two finite branch points of cycle type (r,1r−1)(r,1^{r-1}), and a full (2​r−1)(2r-1)-cycle at infinity; Riemann–Hurwitz is exact, 2​(r−1)+(2​r−2)=2​(2​r−1)−22(r-1)+(2r-2)=2(2r-1)-2. By Cor 6.4 the cover is indecomposable, hence primitive.

Suppose r≥4r\geq 4. A finite inertia generator is an rr-cycle fixing r−1≥3r-1\geq 3 points, so A2​r−1≤MonA_{2r-1}\leq\mathrm{Mon} by [16]. The (2​r−1)(2r-1)-cycle is even, and an rr-cycle is even if and only if rr is odd; so Mon=A2​r−1\mathrm{Mon}=A_{2r-1} for rr odd and Mon=S2​r−1\mathrm{Mon}=S_{2r-1} for rr even.

For r=3r=3 the degree is five and the finite generators are 33-cycles, so A5≤MonA_{5}\leq\mathrm{Mon} by Jordan’s theorem. Every generator is even, so Mon=A5\mathrm{Mon}=A_{5}.

For r=2r=2 the degree is three and the finite generators are transpositions, so Mon=S3\mathrm{Mon}=S_{3}. ∎

Corollary 6.6.

The only members of either family whose quotient cover has solvable monodromy are the maps F2,sF_{2,s}, of generic fibre degree three. They are resolvents in the sense of [21, Thm. 4.4].

Proof.

The cone family has N≥6N\geq 6 with monodromy ANA_{N} or SNS_{N}, and the beta–Hermite family has monodromy A2​r−1A_{2r-1} or S2​r−1S_{2r-1}; these are nonsolvable for 2​r−1≥52r-1\geq 5, that is for r≥3r\geq 3. The remaining case is r=2r=2, where the group is S3S_{3}. ∎

Corollary 6.7.

Let FF be a member of either family of generic fibre degree at least five, or the alternating shear map F12F_{12}. Then the generic inverse branches of FF are not expressible by radicals over the target function field.

Proof.

By Lem 2.5 the extension attached to FF is the purely transcendental base change of the quotient extension along the adjunction of L=x​ΛL=x\Lambda, so the two have the same geometric normal closure group. By Thm 6.1, Thm 6.5 and Thm 5.5 that group is AnA_{n} or SnS_{n} with n≥5n\geq 5, hence nonsolvable. Then we apply the Galois criterion. ∎

Remark 7.7.

Both assertions of Prop 7.4 are instances of Sec. 3.7. Part (3) is Propositions 7.4 and 7.6. Since E∘​(ℚ¯)E^{\circ}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) is infinite, (1) gives infinitely many geometric graded orbits. The generic fibre of JJ has six points by (3), and (1)–(2) identify them as six distinct graded lifts of one unpointed quotient class. ∎

8.2. The bound-preserving gauge group

Assign uu and vv the levels ℓ⁡(u)=1\ell(u)=1 and ℓ⁡(v)=2\ell(v)=2, so that the lift conditions read ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 on AA and ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 on BB. A plane substitution acts on the box only if it preserves both the level filtration and the ordinary total degree. Put

The leading-form reduction used in the bounded scheme, as imported from [21, Prop. 10.13], applies to the box (4,3,1)(4,3,1) and makes the thirty-nine lower-stratum charts and five exact leading cells used below an exhaustive cover after the stated Rabinowitsch localizations.

Assume Hypothesis 8.4. For every field KK of characteristic zero, put DK=Spec⁡K⁡[η]/(η2)D_{K}=\Spec K[\eta]/(\eta^{2}). There is an explicit 𝒢K\mathcal{G}_{K}-equivariant isomorphism

The triple (A⋆,B⋆,Λ⋆)(A_{\star},B_{\star},\Lambda_{\star}) of [4] lies in the box with exact degrees (4,3,1)(4,3,1) and μ⁡(A⋆,B⋆,Λ⋆)=27\mu(A_{\star},B_{\star},\Lambda_{\star})=27, and is defined over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. By Thm 8.5 it lies in the 𝒢⁡(ℚ)\mathcal{G}(\mathbb{Q})-orbit of (A0,B0,Λ0)(A_{0},B_{0},\Lambda_{0}); the ratio of the two Keller constants is accounted for by Lem 8.2.

8.4. The global proof

Proof of Thm 8.5.

Assume Hypothesis 8.4. All formulas below are defined over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, so it suffices to construct the isomorphism over ℚ\mathbb{Q} and base change; emptiness statements established by unit ideals over ℚ\mathbb{Q} likewise hold over every KK.

First, the strata and the reduced support. Besides the exact stratum, the box contains the lower actual-degree strata with (d1,d2,d3)≤(4,3,1)(d_{1},d_{2},d_{3})\leq(4,3,1) coordinatewise and (d1,d2,d3)≠(4,3,1)(d_{1},d_{2},d_{3})\neq(4,3,1). Exact descending characteristic-zero elimination covers these strata by thirty-nine coordinate charts and closes each with a unit ideal, so every such stratum is empty. On the exact stratum, the five exact leading-cell eliminations show that every geometric point lies in the 𝒢\mathcal{G}-orbit of (A0,B0,Λ0)(A_{0},B_{0},\Lambda_{0}) and that the scheme-theoretic stabilizer of that point is trivial. Since the orbit contains the ℚ\mathbb{Q}-point (A0,B0,Λ0)(A_{0},B_{0},\Lambda_{0}), the reduced scheme is the trivial 𝒢\mathcal{G}-torsor, hence isomorphic to 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

Second, the formal slice. The 27×2527\times 25 Jacobian of the equations Eq. 28 at (A0,B0,Λ0)(A_{0},B_{0},\Lambda_{0}) has rank 1818; its kernel has dimension seven and contains the six-dimensional tangent space of the 𝒢\mathcal{G}-orbit. The formal-slice elimination identifies the completed local ring at the normal form as

𝒪^𝒴1,2,(4,3,1)∘,(A0,B0,Λ0)≅K⁡[[β1,…,β6,t]]/(t2),\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{1,2,(4,3,1)},\,(A_{0},B_{0},\Lambda_{0})}\;\cong\;K[[\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{6},t]]/(t^{2}),

where the βi\beta_{i} are the six gauge directions and tt spans the transverse line. The independent global dual parameter η\eta satisfies the exact bridge identity t=−15224​ηt=-\tfrac{15}{224}\eta. In particular the transverse slice is a square-zero thickening of the normal form, that is, a DKD_{K}-point of 𝒴1,2,(4,3,1)∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{1,2,(4,3,1)} supported at (A0,B0,Λ0)(A_{0},B_{0},\Lambda_{0}). Explicitly, writing

A˙=12​u3+15​u2​v+1730​u2+25​u​v+15​v,B˙=u2+25​u​v+415​u+25​v,\begin{split}\dot{A}&=\tfrac{1}{2}u^{3}+\tfrac{1}{5}u^{2}v+\tfrac{17}{30}u^{2}+\tfrac{2}{5}uv+\tfrac{1}{5}v,\\ \dot{B}&=u^{2}+\tfrac{2}{5}uv+\tfrac{4}{15}u+\tfrac{2}{5}v,\end{split}

one has

μ⁡(A0−15224​η​A˙,B0−15224​η​B˙,Λ0)=2−116​η(modη2),\mu\bigl(A_{0}-\tfrac{15}{224}\eta\dot{A},\ B_{0}-\tfrac{15}{224}\eta\dot{B},\ \Lambda_{0}\bigr)=2-\tfrac{1}{16}\eta\pmod{\eta^{2}},

a unit in K⁡[η]/(η2)K[\eta]/(\eta^{2}), and the three leading coefficients remain units, so the displayed family is the required DKD_{K}-point.

Third, the action map. Translating the slice DKD_{K}-point by the group defines

α:𝒢K×DK⟶𝒴1,2,(4,3,1),K∘.\alpha\colon\mathcal{G}_{K}\times D_{K}\longrightarrow\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{1,2,(4,3,1),K}.

By the first step, α\alpha is an isomorphism on reduced schemes; by equivariance and transitivity on the reduction, the comparison of completed local rings at an arbitrary point reduces to the normal form, where the second step gives an isomorphism. Hence α\alpha is flat and unramified, that is, étale. Since its reduction is an isomorphism, every geometric fibre is a single reduced point; therefore α\alpha is universally injective, hence radicial. An étale radicial surjection is an isomorphism. Renaming the transverse coordinate as η\eta gives the asserted product decomposition, with 𝒢K\mathcal{G}_{K} acting by left translation on the orbit factor and trivially on the transverse one. ∎

Remark 8.7.

The identification t=−15224​ηt=-\tfrac{15}{224}\eta of the global nilpotent with the intrinsic formal-slice parameter is an exact bridge identity; we attach no arithmetic significance to the constant.

The quotient map of the normal form is (P,Q)=(Λ0​B0,Λ02​A0)(P,Q)=(\Lambda_{0}B_{0},\Lambda_{0}^{2}A_{0}), with Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)=2​Λ02\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)=2\Lambda_{0}^{2} as Cor 2.4 requires at κ=2\kappa=2. The substitution

Remark 8.8.

The branch curve of the flagship quotient is the irreducible cubic Γf={P3−P2−18PQ+27Q2+16Q=0}\Gamma_{f}=\{P^{3}-P^{2}-18PQ+27Q^{2}+16Q=0\}. It has a single singular point, at (P,Q)=(43,427)(P,Q)=(\tfrac{4}{3},\tfrac{4}{27}), where the quadratic part is 3​(p−3​q)23(p-3q)^{2} in the local coordinates p=P−43p=P-\tfrac{4}{3}, q=Q−427q=Q-\tfrac{4}{27}; the point is therefore a cusp. m⟼(43−3​(1−3​m)2,427−3​m​(1−3​m)2),m\longmapsto\Bigl(\tfrac{4}{3}-3(1-3m)^{2},\ \tfrac{4}{27}-3m(1-3m)^{2}\Bigr),

of degrees two and three, so both the semigroup at infinity and the local value semigroup at the cusp are ⟨2,3⟩\langle 2,3\rangle in the sense of Sec. 2.4.

Remark 8.9.

Passing to the multiprojective bounded scheme, that is, taking the quotient by the three coefficient scalings, replaces 𝒢\mathcal{G} by the three-dimensional group BlinB_{\mathrm{lin}}, and the theorem reads: the multiprojective flagship stratum is Blin,K×DKB_{\mathrm{lin},K}\times D_{K}. The six affine gauge directions of the coefficient incidence calculation are those of Blin×(𝔾m)3B_{\mathrm{lin}}\times(\mathbb{G}_{m})^{3}, not of any nonlinear plane substitution.

9.4. The hyperbolic geography

Corollary 9.5.

For every pair r,s≥1r,s\geq 1 one has 𝒦⁡(3,(1,−r,−s))≠∅\mathcal{K}(3,(1,-r,-s))\neq\emptyset. Thus every three-dimensional unit-positive weight of the form (1,−r,−s)(1,-r,-s) is populated.

Remark 9.6.

The fields of definition are uneven across the geography. The whole unit boundary r=1r=1 is rational, by the 3333-sheeted witness Thm 3.20 at s=1s=1, Sec. 8 at s=2s=2 and Thm 9.2 for s≥3s\geq 3; so is the row r=2r=2, by Prop 4.5(1). For r≥3r\geq 3 the construction of Sec. 4 produces a member over Kr=ℚ⁡(ζ)K_{r}=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta), and Prop 4.5(3) shows that this field is totally imaginary whenever rr is odd. Whether those rows contain rational members is not decided here.

10. Nielsen classes, braid orbits, and arithmetic monodromy

We organize the covers of Sec. 6 by their Nielsen classes and extract the arithmetic that the Hurwitz formalism of [10, 14, 24] attaches to them.

10.1. The Nielsen classes

For a finite group GG and an ℓ\ell-tuple 𝐂=(C1,…,Cℓ)\mathbf{C}=(C_{1},\dots,C_{\ell}) of conjugacy classes, the Nielsen class is

Ni(G,𝐂)={(g1,…,gℓ):gi∈Ci,g1⋯gℓ=1,⟨g1,…,gℓ⟩=G}/∼,\mathrm{Ni}(G,\mathbf{C})=\bigl\{(g_{1},\dots,g_{\ell}):g_{i}\in C_{i},\ g_{1}\cdots g_{\ell}=1,\ \langle g_{1},\dots,g_{\ell}\rangle=G\bigr\}/\!\sim,

modulo simultaneous conjugation, and the components of the Hurwitz space ℋ⁡(G,𝐂)\mathcal{H}(G,\mathbf{C}) over the configuration space 𝒰ℓ\mathcal{U}_{\ell} correspond to the orbits of the Hurwitz braid group HℓH_{\ell} on Ni⁡(G,𝐂)\mathrm{Ni}(G,\mathbf{C}) [14].

For the alternating shear cover, Theorems 5.4 and 5.5 give

(36) Ni⁡(A12,(C36,C(9,3))),ℓ=7,\mathrm{Ni}\bigl(A_{12},\;(C_{3}^{6},C_{(9,3)})\bigr),\qquad\ell=7,

with C3C_{3} the class of 33-cycles and C(9,3)C_{(9,3)} one of the two A12A_{12}-classes of cycle type (9,3)(9,3). For the cyclic cone family at (k,d)(k,d) with kk even, Thm 6.1 and Prop 3.22 give

(37) Ni⁡(AN,(Ck+1d,C(N−1,1))),ℓ=d+1,\mathrm{Ni}\bigl(A_{N},\;(C_{k+1}^{\,d},C_{(N-1,1)})\bigr),\qquad\ell=d+1,

and for kk odd the same shape inside SNS_{N}. For the beta–Hermite family at odd r≥3r\geq 3, Rem 4.7 and Thm 6.5 give

(38) Ni⁡(A2​r−1,(Cr,Cr,C2​r−1)),ℓ=3.\mathrm{Ni}\bigl(A_{2r-1},\;(C_{r},C_{r},C_{2r-1})\bigr),\qquad\ell=3.

10.2. Split pairs

A conjugacy class of SnS_{n} of cycle type λ=(λ1,…,λℓ)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{\ell}) meets AnA_{n} in two classes if and only if the parts of λ\lambda are odd and pairwise distinct, and any odd permutation interchanges them. For such a λ\lambda the integer n−ℓ=∑i(λi−1)n-\ell=\sum_{i}(\lambda_{i}-1) is even, and the two classes are separated by the quadratic field ℚ⁡(m∗)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{m^{*}}) with

(39) m∗=(−1)(n−ℓ)/2λ1⋯λℓ.m^{*}=(-1)^{(n-\ell)/2}\lambda_{1}\cdots\lambda_{\ell}.
Lemma 10.1.

Among the classes of Sec. 10.1, exactly the classes at infinity split. Their split-pair fields are

(9,3)⊂A12​(shear):m∗=(−1)5⋅27=−27,ℚ⁡(−3);(N−1,1)⊂AN​(k​even):m∗=(−1)(N−2)/2​(N−1);(5,1)⊂A6​(six-sheeted):m∗=(−1)2⋅5=5,ℚ⁡(5);(2​r−1)⊂A2​r−1​(r​odd):m∗=(−1)r−1​(2​r−1)=2​r−1.\begin{split}(9,3)\subset A_{12}\ \text{(shear)}:&\quad m^{*}=(-1)^{5}\cdot 27=-27,\quad\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3});\\ (N-1,1)\subset A_{N}\ (k\ \text{even}):&\quad m^{*}=(-1)^{(N-2)/2}(N-1);\\ (5,1)\subset A_{6}\ \text{(six-sheeted)}:&\quad m^{*}=(-1)^{2}\cdot 5=5,\quad\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5});\\ (2r-1)\subset A_{2r-1}\ (r\ \text{odd}):&\quad m^{*}=(-1)^{r-1}(2r-1)=2r-1.\end{split}

In particular the finite classes C3C_{3}, Ck+1C_{k+1} and CrC_{r} do not split, since each has the part 11 with multiplicity at least two.

Proof.

For Ck+1C_{k+1} the type is (k+1,1N−k−1)(k+1,1^{N-k-1}) with N−k−1=k⁡(d−1)−1≥3N-k-1=k(d-1)-1\geq 3 by Cor 3.7, and for CrC_{r} it is (r,1r−1)(r,1^{r-1}) with r−1≥2r-1\geq 2; the part 11 repeats in both, as it does for C3⊂A12C_{3}\subset A_{12}. The four displayed types have distinct odd parts, and Eq. 39 gives the values shown. For the last, rr odd makes (−1)r−1=1(-1)^{r-1}=1; at r=3r=3 the field is ℚ⁡(5)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5}). ∎

By the branch cycle lemma [10, 24], if a cover in one of these Nielsen classes is defined over a field FF with geometric group AnA_{n}, and the branch point carrying the split class is FF-rational, then either FF contains the split-pair field, or the arithmetic monodromy group is SnS_{n} and the constants extension is exactly that field.

Proposition 10.2.

The six-sheeted map of Thm 3.19 and the map F3F_{3} of Prop 4.5(2) are both defined over K=ℚ⁡(−15)K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-15}), which contains neither 5\sqrt{5} nor −3\sqrt{-3}. Their classes at infinity are (5,1)⊂A6(5,1)\subset A_{6} and (5)⊂A5(5)\subset A_{5}, with split-pair field ℚ⁡(5)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5}) in both cases, and in both cases the point at infinity is rational. Hence both covers have arithmetic monodromy SnS_{n} over KK, their constant field extension relative to KK is K⁡(5)/K,K(\sqrt{5})/K, of degree two, and their full constant field is K⁡(5)=ℚ⁡(−15,5),K(\sqrt{5})=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-15},\sqrt{5}), of degree four over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

Proof.

The fields of definition are Thm 3.19 and Prop 4.5(2), and the classes at infinity are Prop 3.22 at (k,d)=(2,3)(k,d)=(2,3) and Rem 4.7 at p=3p=3. Their split-pair fields are ℚ⁡(5)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5}) by Lem 10.1. That 5∉K\sqrt{5}\notin K and −3∉K\sqrt{-3}\notin K holds because KK is quadratic over ℚ\mathbb{Q} with discriminant class −15-15, and 55, −3-3, −15-15 lie in distinct classes of ℚ×/(ℚ×)2\mathbb{Q}^{\times}/(\mathbb{Q}^{\times})^{2}.

The geometric monodromy is AnA_{n} by Thm 6.1 at k=2k=2 even and Thm 6.5 at p=3p=3 odd. The branch point at infinity is KK-rational, and its class is one of the two split classes; by the branch cycle lemma [10, 24], a KK-model with geometric group AnA_{n} whose split class sits at a KK-rational branch point either has 5∈K\sqrt{5}\in K, which fails, or has arithmetic monodromy SnS_{n} with constant field extension generated by 5\sqrt{5}. Hence the arithmetic group is SnS_{n} and the relative constant extension is K⁡(5)/KK(\sqrt{5})/K, which has degree two since 5∉K\sqrt{5}\notin K. The full constant field is therefore K⁡(5)=ℚ⁡(−15,5)K(\sqrt{5})=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-15},\sqrt{5}). ∎

Remark 10.3.

The unpointed six-sheeted quotient cover descends to ℚ\mathbb{Q}, with seed φ0=W2+W3\varphi_{0}=W^{2}+W^{3}. That model is a different object from the two graded maps above: its constant field is the split-pair field ℚ⁡(5)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5}) itself, whereas the graded maps, being defined over KK, acquire the compositum K⁡(5)K(\sqrt{5}).

Remark 10.4.

Proposition 10.2 accounts for the factor 55 in −15-15, but not for the factor −3-3: no class attached to either of those two covers has split-pair field ℚ⁡(−3)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3}). The field ℚ⁡(−3)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3}) arises in this paper only from the (9,3)(9,3)-class of the degree-twelve shear cover, which is a different cover in a different family. The identity −15=5⋅(−3)-15=5\cdot(-3) therefore records that ℚ⁡(−15)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-15}) is the third quadratic subfield of ℚ⁡(5,−3)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5},\sqrt{-3}), and no mechanism in this paper connects the two factors. Since −15​5=5​−3\sqrt{-15}\sqrt{5}=5\sqrt{-3}, that biquadratic field is exactly the constant field ℚ⁡(−15,5)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-15},\sqrt{5}) of Prop 10.2, so the coincidence lives in the constant field the two covers acquire.

10.3. Arithmetic monodromy of the alternating shear cover

Lemma 10.5.

For s,t∈ℂ×s,t\in\mathbb{C}^{\times} the substitution X↦s​XX\mapsto sX, Y↦t​YY\mapsto tY, P↦s−1​PP\mapsto s^{-1}P carries the cover Eq. 23 with parameters (c,d)(c,d) to the cover with parameters (c​s−2​t3,d​s2​t−1)(cs^{-2}t^{3},\,ds^{2}t^{-1}). The action of this torus on {cd≠0}\{cd\neq 0\} is simply transitive up to a group of order four, so every member with c​d≠0cd\neq 0 becomes the normalised member c=d=1c=d=1, which is defined over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

Proof.

The first term of Eq. 23 is XX with coefficient one, which fixes the rescaling of PP to be by s−1s^{-1}. Matching the terms 2​c​X−1​Y32cX^{-1}Y^{3} and 6​c​d​X​Y26cdXY^{2} then gives c↦c​s−2​t3c\mapsto cs^{-2}t^{3} and c​d↦c​d​t2cd\mapsto cdt^{2}, whence d↦d​s2​t−1d\mapsto ds^{2}t^{-1}; the remaining nine terms match, since each is cα​dβ​Xi​Yjc^{\alpha}d^{\beta}X^{i}Y^{j} with −2​α+2​β+i−1=0-2\alpha+2\beta+i-1=0 and 3​α−β+j=03\alpha-\beta+j=0. Given (c,d)(c,d) with c​d≠0cd\neq 0, the equations c​s−2​t3=1cs^{-2}t^{3}=1 and d​s2​t−1=1ds^{2}t^{-1}=1 give t2=(c​d)−1t^{2}=(cd)^{-1} and s2=(c/d)1/2s^{2}=(c/d)^{1/2}, solvable over ℂ\mathbb{C}; the stabilizer of (1,1)(1,1) is {(s,t):t=s2,t2=1}\{(s,t):t=s^{2},\,t^{2}=1\}, of order four. ∎

Theorem 10.6.

The normalised cover P⁡(X,Y)P(X,Y) at c=d=1c=d=1 is defined over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, its geometric monodromy group is A12A_{12}, its arithmetic monodromy group over ℚ⁡(Y)\mathbb{Q}(Y) is S12S_{12}, and the constants extension is exactly ℚ⁡(−3)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3}).

Proof.

The geometric group is A12A_{12} by Thm 5.5, whose proof uses only c​d≠0cd\neq 0. Let ℘\wp denote the target coordinate, so that the fibre of the cover is cut out by the degree-twelve polynomial X3​(P⁡(X,Y)−℘)X^{3}\bigl(P(X,Y)-\wp\bigr) in XX; it has degree twelve and nonzero constant term −c23​Y6-\tfrac{c^{2}}{3}Y^{6}, so its roots are exactly the twelve points of the fibre. Exact elimination at c=d=1c=d=1 gives

(40) discX⁡[X3​(P⁡(X,Y)−℘)]=−27​Y12​RΓ​(℘,Y)2,\operatorname{disc}_{X}\bigl[X^{3}\bigl(P(X,Y)-\wp\bigr)\bigr]=-27\,Y^{12}R_{\Gamma}(\wp,Y)^{2},

with RΓR_{\Gamma} the irreducible polynomial defining the branch curve Γ\Gamma.

Since A12A_{12} has index two in S12S_{12}, the constants extension of the normal closure is generated by the square root of this discriminant. Modulo squares in ℚ​(Y,℘)×\mathbb{Q}(Y,\wp)^{\times} the right-hand side of Eq. 40 is −27≡−3-27\equiv-3, which is not a square. Hence the arithmetic group is not contained in A12A_{12}, so it equals S12S_{12}, and the constants extension is ℚ⁡(−3)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3}). ∎

Remark 10.7.

Theorem 10.6 agrees with the branch cycle lemma: the branch point at infinity is ℚ\mathbb{Q}-rational and its class has split-pair field ℚ⁡(−3)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3}) by Lem 10.1, so a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-model with geometric group A12A_{12} must acquire exactly this constants extension. The discriminant computation is the independent verification. The same comparison applied to the two covers of Prop 10.2 predicts 55 modulo squares for the discriminant of the normalised six-sheeted map over ℚ⁡(−15)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-15}) and for that of Eq. 17 in ρ\rho at p=3p=3 over K3​(P,Q)K_{3}(P,Q).

Corollary 10.8.

Let F=ℚ⁡(−3)F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3}) and let L~\widetilde{L} be the Galois closure of F⁡(X,Y)F(X,Y) over F⁡(℘,Y)F(\wp,Y). Then L~/F⁡(℘,Y)\widetilde{L}/F(\wp,Y) is a regular realisation of A12A_{12} over F⁡(Y)F(Y) with the seven-point ramification of Eq. 36. Viewed over ℚ⁡(℘,Y)\mathbb{Q}(\wp,Y), the same normal closure has arithmetic group S12S_{12} and full constant field FF; it is therefore not regular over ℚ⁡(Y)\mathbb{Q}(Y).

Proof.

By Thm 10.6, adjoining FF kills the unique discriminant square class and leaves geometric group A12A_{12}; since FF is the full constant field, the resulting A12A_{12}-extension is regular over F⁡(Y)F(Y). Before the constant extension the arithmetic group is S12S_{12} but the algebraic closure of ℚ\mathbb{Q} in the normal closure is FF, which is exactly the failure of regularity over ℚ⁡(Y)\mathbb{Q}(Y). ∎

10.5. Modular tower level structure

The classes of the shear family, of the cone family at kk even, and of the beta–Hermite family at rr odd all consist of elements of odd order, hence of 2′2^{\prime}-elements; the cone family at kk odd is excluded, since there Ck+1C_{k+1} has even order. For the classes that do qualify, the Nielsen class is the level-zero layer of a 22-Frattini Modular Tower in the sense of [11, 5]: the tower of Hurwitz spaces attached to the characteristic quotients of the universal 22-Frattini cover of ANA_{N}, with the classes lifted canonically by Schur–Zassenhaus. A level-zero component supports a nonempty level one only if its tuples lift to the central spin extension with product one; for genus-zero covers with all ramification indices odd this obstruction is Serre’s [20]

(41) ω=∑PeP2−18mod2,\omega=\sum_{P}\frac{e_{P}^{2}-1}{8}\ \bmod 2,

the sum over ramified points, the component being obstructed if and only if ω=1\omega=1.

Proposition 10.10.

The following hold.

  1. (1)

    The alternating shear class has ω=6+10+1≡1\omega=6+10+1\equiv 1: its component is 22-Frattini obstructed and the Modular Tower above it is empty.

  2. (2)

    The class ((3,13)3;(5,1))\bigl((3,1^{3})^{3};(5,1)\bigr) of the six-sheeted map has ω=3+3≡0\omega=3+3\equiv 0: its component is unobstructed, its spin lifts lie in ⋅A6≅SL2​(9)2\!\cdot\!A_{6}\cong\mathrm{SL}_{2}(9), and level one of its tower is nonempty.

  3. (3)

    For the beta–Hermite family at odd rr, ω≡(r−1)/2mod2\omega\equiv(r-1)/2\bmod 2, so the component is obstructed if and only if r≡3(mod4)r\equiv 3\pmod{4}.

Only points with eP>1e_{P}>1 contribute to Eq. 41. For (1) the six finite branch values each carry one point with eP=3e_{P}=3, contributing 6⋅16\cdot 1, and infinity carries eP=9e_{P}=9 and eP=3e_{P}=3, contributing 10+110+1; the total is 1717. For (2) the three finite branch values contribute 3⋅13\cdot 1 and infinity contributes (25−1)/8=3(25-1)/8=3; the total is 66. For (3) the two finite branch values contribute 2​(r2−1)/82(r^{2}-1)/8 and infinity contributes ((2​r−1)2−1)/8\bigl((2r-1)^{2}-1\bigr)/8, so

ω=2​(r2−1)+4​r2−4​r8=(3​r+1)​(r−1)4.\omega=\frac{2(r^{2}-1)+4r^{2}-4r}{8}=\frac{(3r+1)(r-1)}{4}.

Writing r=2​m+1r=2m+1 gives ω=m⁡(3​m+2)≡m2≡m(mod2)\omega=m(3m+2)\equiv m^{2}\equiv m\pmod{2}, and m=(r−1)/2m=(r-1)/2 is odd exactly when r≡3(mod4)r\equiv 3\pmod{4}. ∎

Thus F3,sF_{3,s} and the shear map sit on dead branches, while the six-sheeted map and F5,sF_{5,s} sit on live ones.

Theorem 10.11.

The cone classes Eq. 37 and the beta–Hermite classes Eq. 38 are pure-cycle of genus zero, and each carries a single inner braid orbit once a split class is fixed. Precisely:

  1. (1)

    for kk odd, Ni⁡(SN,(Ck+1d,C(N−1,1)))\mathrm{Ni}\bigl(S_{N},(C_{k+1}^{\,d},C_{(N-1,1)})\bigr) is a single braid orbit;

  2. (2)

    for kk even, the finite class does not split, the class at infinity splits in ANA_{N}, each of the two split classes carries a single inner braid orbit, and the two are exchanged by odd conjugation and form one absolute component;

  3. (3)

    for rr even, Ni⁡(S2​r−1,(Cr,Cr,C2​r−1))\mathrm{Ni}\bigl(S_{2r-1},(C_{r},C_{r},C_{2r-1})\bigr) is a single braid orbit;

  4. (4)

    for rr odd, each of the two split full-cycle classes in A2​r−1A_{2r-1} carries a single inner braid orbit, and the two form one absolute component.

In every case the corresponding Hurwitz component is irreducible.

Proof.

Every class occurring in Eq. 37 and Eq. 38 is a single cycle together with fixed points, so the data are pure-cycle, and the Riemann–Hurwitz equalities

d⁡((k+1)−1)+((N−1)−1)=k​d+N−2=2​N−2,2​(r−1)+((2​r−1)−1)=4​r−4=2​(2​r−1)−2,\begin{split}d\bigl((k+1)-1\bigr)+\bigl((N-1)-1\bigr)&=kd+N-2=2N-2,\\ 2(r-1)+\bigl((2r-1)-1\bigr)&=4r-4=2(2r-1)-2,\end{split}

are exact, so the genus is zero. Liu–Osserman [17, Thm. 1.2] prove irreducibility of a genus-zero pure-cycle Hurwitz space for an arbitrary number of branch points and arbitrary cycle lengths subject only to that equality; even lengths are permitted. Hence the absolute Nielsen class in SnS_{n} is a single braid orbit in all four cases.

In cases (1) and (3) the monodromy group is SnS_{n} by Thm 6.1 and Thm 6.5, the prescribed classes are SnS_{n}-classes, and Z⁡(Sn)=1Z(S_{n})=1, so the absolute and inner Nielsen classes coincide and the statement is the displayed irreducibility.

In cases (2) and (4) the group is AnA_{n}, and by Lem 10.1 exactly the class at infinity splits, into C+C^{+} and C−C^{-}. Fix C+C^{+}. Conjugation by an odd permutation carries Ni⁡(An,(…,C+))\mathrm{Ni}\bigl(A_{n},(\dots,C^{+})\bigr) bijectively onto Ni⁡(An,(…,C−))\mathrm{Ni}\bigl(A_{n},(\dots,C^{-})\bigr) and commutes with the braid action; and no tuple with last entry in C+C^{+} is carried to another such tuple by an odd element, since odd conjugation moves C+C^{+} to C−C^{-}. The absolute Nielsen class is therefore in braid-equivariant bijection with the inner class at C+C^{+}, so a single absolute orbit is a single inner orbit on each fixed split class, and the two are exchanged as asserted. ∎

At p=3p=3 case (4) is Prop 10.9, computed there independently by the rigidity count.

The shear class Eq. 36 is not pure-cycle, its class at infinity having two nontrivial cycles, so Thm 10.11 does not reach it and its component count is a direct computation.

Lemma 10.12.

Let n≥6n\geq 6. A transitive subgroup of SnS_{n} generated by 33-cycles is AnA_{n}.

Proof.

Let HH be such a subgroup. It is primitive. Indeed, suppose that a nontrivial block system existed. A 33-cycle cannot move one block to a different block: if a block has more than one point, moving it setwise would move at least four points, while a 33-cycle has support three. Hence every generating 33-cycle fixes every block setwise, so the group they generate cannot be transitive across more than one block. This contradiction proves primitivity. Jordan’s theorem now gives An≤HA_{n}\leq H, because HH contains a 33-cycle and n≥6n\geq 6. Every generator is even, so H≤AnH\leq A_{n}, and equality follows. ∎

Irreducibility of a component does not by itself imply that the graded Keller family sweeps it, and the two can differ in dimension.

Remark 10.14.

The six-sheeted family has ℓ=4\ell=4, so its reduced Hurwitz space is a curve over the jj-line, the setting of [5]. The lift conditions of Thm 3.19 freeze the seed up to conjugation, so the graded Keller condition selects a Gal⁡(ℚ¯/ℚ)\Gal(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})-stable pair of normalised seeds, conjugate over ℚ⁡(−15)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-15}). The two share a single unpointed quotient-cover class, defined over ℚ\mathbb{Q}; what fails to descend is the lift-point marking, the two markings giving distinct 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp}-orbits with field of moduli ℚ⁡(−15)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-15}). The obstruction therefore lies in the pointed structure and not in the cover, so it is invisible on the coarse Hurwitz space.

Remark 10.15.

The six-sheeted component is unobstructed, so level one of its tower is a nonempty Hurwitz space for the first characteristic 22-Frattini quotient of A6A_{6}. Does any graded Keller map realise a level-one cover, or do graded Keller maps occur only at level zero? Either answer is a Modular-Tower-type finiteness statement for the Keller condition.

11. Compactification and intersection theory of the alternating shear curve

By Prop 10.16 the alternating shear locus is a curve in the fourfold ℋrd\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{rd}}, and the concluding question of that section was what cuts it out. This section answers the local question unconditionally: the locus is an explicit codimension-three rational local complete intersection in a birational coefficient chart. Assuming Hypothesis 11.3, its normalised admissible-cover closure is an orbicurve with thirteen boundary points and its rational one-cycle class on the compactified branch space is determined.

Proof.

The resultant, the discriminant factorisation, separability, irreducibility and coprimality are exact computations; the conditional identification of the two Galois groups is Hypothesis 11.3(H3). For the collision counts, the branch values come in involution pairs ±μ\pm\mu since PτP_{\tau} is odd; a coincidence μi=μj\mu_{i}=\mu_{j} within the even part forces the conjugate coincidence −μi=−μj-\mu_{i}=-\mu_{j} and contributes τ\tau-multiplicity four to the discriminant, while a coincidence μi=−μj\mu_{i}=-\mu_{j} between the two parts is self-conjugate and contributes multiplicity two. The certified multiplicities 22 on CC and 44 on D4D_{4} therefore give one and two nodes respectively. ∎

Remark 11.7.

What remains open is the full rank-three parabolic and logarithmic splitting of the normal bundle NN, including the stabilizer characters at the thirteen orbifold points and the extension classes; Thm 11.6 determines only its determinant. The coefficient-stack splitting obtained after the substitution τ=t4\tau=t^{4} is a computation in a different ambient space and should not be identified with the normal bundle on the normalised admissible cover stack.

12. Fields of definition

We return to the cyclic cone family of Sec. 3 and determine over which fields a seed exists. The first lift condition of Eq. 10 is linear and imposes nothing on the field. The second is the vanishing of the lift form 𝒬(k)\mathcal{Q}^{(k)} of Eq. 11, a form of degree kk in the seed coefficients with rational coefficients, and it is the arithmetic obstruction.

12.1. The form at level two

At k=2k=2, writing φ=∑j=2ncj​Wj\varphi=\sum_{j=2}^{n}c_{j}W^{j},

12.2. Real obstruction and odd levels

Theorem 12.2.

The following hold.

  1. (1)

    Let kk be even and let KK admit a real embedding. Then no seed at level kk exists over KK. Consequently the coefficient field of every member of Sec. 3 with kk even is totally imaginary.

φ​(W)kW2=−W2​k−2​(1+2​W2​k−1)k.\frac{\varphi(W)^{k}}{W^{2}}=-W^{2k-2}\bigl(1+2W^{2k-1}\bigr)^{k}.

Write Rm=Wm+2​(1−W)mR_{m}=W^{m+2}(1-W)^{m}, which vanishes to order m+2m+2 at W=0W=0 and to order mm at W=1W=1; hence Dj​RmD^{j}R_{m} vanishes at both endpoints for j≤m−1j\leq m-1. For 0≤j<m0\leq j<m, integration by parts mm times gives

Corollary 12.5.

𝒬3≅⟨3,5⟩\mathcal{Q}_{3}\cong\langle 3,5\rangle and 𝒬4≅⟨3,5,7⟩\mathcal{Q}_{4}\cong\langle 3,5,7\rangle. The first three norms are h0=13h_{0}=\tfrac{1}{3}, h1=180h_{1}=\tfrac{1}{80} and h2=11575h_{2}=\tfrac{1}{1575}, congruent to 33, 55 and 77; the discriminant of ⟨3,5⟩\langle 3,5\rangle is −60≡−15-60\equiv-15. Over ℝ\mathbb{R} the form is positive definite. For p∤210p\nmid 210, every nondegenerate ternary form over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} is isotropic, and a smooth zero lifts. At p=3p=3 and p=5p=5 the unit ratios −5/7≡1(mod3)-5/7\equiv 1\pmod{3} and −7/3≡1(mod5)-7/3\equiv 1\pmod{5} are squares, so already the binary parts 5​y2+7​z25y^{2}+7z^{2} and 3​x2+7​z23x^{2}+7z^{2} are isotropic. At p=2p=2 take y=3y=3, z=1z=1 and solve

At p=7p=7 reduction forces x≡y≡0(mod7)x\equiv y\equiv 0\pmod{7}, since −5/3≡3-5/3\equiv 3 is a nonsquare modulo 77, and a valuation descent rules out a primitive solution. The two anisotropic places {7,∞}\{7,\infty\} have even cardinality, as Hilbert reciprocity requires. ∎

By Thm 3.19 the six-sheeted map is defined over ℚ⁡(−15)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-15}), and the two roots a,a¯=−3−aa,\bar{a}=-3-a of c22+3​c2+6c_{2}^{2}+3c_{2}+6 give two maps interchanged by Gal⁡(ℚ⁡(−15)/ℚ)\Gal(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-15})/\mathbb{Q}). Its field of moduli, as a 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp}-orbit in 𝒴1,1,(8,14,1)∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{1,1,(8,14,1)}, is ℚ\mathbb{Q} or ℚ⁡(−15)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-15}) according as the two conjugate maps are 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp}-equivalent over ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}.

Proposition 12.6.

Let φ=a​W2+(1−a)​W3\varphi=aW^{2}+(1-a)W^{3} with a2+3​a+6=0a^{2}+3a+6=0. Then Π⁡(W,0)\Pi(W,0) has the two nonzero roots

W=1andβ=2−a4,W=1\quad\text{and}\quad\beta=\frac{2-a}{4},
